title: Debating fixed links for Scotland’s islands
label: 27 October 2026 · Backbench debates: island fixed links
summary: Patricia Ferguson asked the Backbench Business Committee for a three‑hour Chamber debate on building fixed links—mainly tunnels—between some of Scotland’s islands. She argued ferries are unreliable and costly, harming island life, services and businesses; pointed to the Faroe Islands’ experience and recent funding for Shetland tunnel planning; and said while transport is devolved the scale and security implications mean the UK Government will likely need to help. The Committee will consider timing, with Patricia preferring a Chamber debate over Westminster Hall.

speakers.label: Patricia Ferguson
speakers.name: Patricia Ferguson
speakers.role: MP and member of the Scottish Affairs Committee

glossary.definition: A permanent road or rail connection—usually a bridge or tunnel—between islands or to the mainland.
A tunnel built under the sea to connect landmasses without using ferries.
A proposed spaceport on Unst in Shetland, mentioned as an example where good links matter for security and industry.
A secondary debating chamber in the UK Parliament, used when a full Chamber debate isn’t possible.
The devolved government in Scotland responsible for most transport decisions there.
An autonomous North Atlantic territory of Denmark whose inter‑island tunnels were cited as a positive example.

chapters.title: Asking for a Chamber debate
chapters.takeaway: Patricia asked for a three‑hour Chamber debate to examine fixed links for Scotland’s islands and said cross‑party interest exists.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re considering applications for debates. Patricia Ferguson has asked for a three‑hour Chamber debate on fixed‑link connectivity in Scotland’s islands. Patricia, please present your case.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: Thank you. This matter came to our Scottish Affairs Committee after a visit to Unst to see the SaxaVord spaceport. Locals were enthusiastic about tunnels and other fixed links.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: The Committee has visited islands, spoken to residents, and found a strong case for at least debating fixed links: life and business on the islands face intolerable limitations.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: We’ve published a report and seen practical proposals—Shetland recently got £23 million from the Scottish Government to develop inter‑island tunnel plans—so now is a timely moment for a discussion in the House.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Jamie, you had a question about the forum for this debate.

turns.speaker: Jamie Stone
turns.text: You asked for a Chamber debate, but there’s a long waiting list. Would you accept a Westminster Hall debate to move this forward sooner, or do you want to hold out for the Chamber?

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: We’d prefer the Chamber. It attracts more members and gives a more critical, cross‑House examination. But if scheduling means Westminster Hall, we’d understand.

chapters.title: Why fixed links are being considered
chapters.takeaway: Ferry unreliability, high costs and social impacts—backed by the Faroes example—drive support for tunnels and other permanent links.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: Ferries are often unreliable. Weather, distance and geography make travel difficult. On our visit to Unst we needed three ferries and a long minibus trip just to reach the island.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: That affects everyday life: simple things like going to a doctor or the cinema require planning. Businesses face high costs and extra logistics when bringing materials or workers to the islands.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: For childbirth, some islanders must travel to Glasgow two weeks before the due date. The health board pays £60 a night for accommodation, which rarely covers real costs and adds strain on families.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: We saw the Faroe Islands’ tunnels stop depopulation there. Their approach aims to keep services accessible so people don’t face long commutes; that experience is persuasive for Scotland’s islands.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: This is about more than transport. It affects the economy, security and the ability of people to live and work on the islands—especially as places like SaxaVord develop.

chapters.title: Devolved responsibility, costs and possible funding
chapters.takeaway: Transport is devolved to Scotland, but the scale and cost of tunnels mean UK involvement is likely; different funding models exist, including state‑backed loans.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Transport is devolved. What do you hope the debate will achieve here, given the Scottish Government has the main decision‑making power?

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: We accept transport is devolved, but the cost of subsea tunnels is immense. The UK Government will probably need to be involved financially and strategically, and they should want to be.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: The UK has security and economic reasons to care: access to a spaceport like SaxaVord, delivering the Government’s aim of opportunity in every postcode, and supporting island industries.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: We aren’t prescribing a single funding model. The Faroes used loans underwritten by Denmark—that’s one option. The point is the scale demands broader discussion, including UK support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The Clerks will be in touch about scheduling. If you’re willing to accept Westminster Hall that doesn’t stop you asking for a Chamber debate later.

turns.speaker: Patricia Ferguson
turns.text: Thank you. We’d like the Chamber but will engage if a Westminster Hall slot is the best way to raise the issue sooner.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That completes the public business. The Committee will now consider the application in private.
